reveal.text: The missing conditions are a to-do list for the owner and steward, and a badge follows when the list is empty.
Ownership coverage, here 25 of 40, is one of the counts a governance process tracks, since it shows where the work remains.

lessons.orientation: Assign governance roles, sort metadata, and turn a policy into a control.
lessons.nextAction: You can now declare a grain and model history, build and test layered models, define metrics once, trace lineage, measure quality, read a contract, classify and protect personal data, and say who owns what.

blocks.text: A company has a rule that customer data is deleted after 36 months. The rule is in a policy document that was approved by a committee, and nobody can say whether it is followed, because nobody is responsible for the table, nothing runs the deletion, and no check would notice if it stopped.

**Data governance** closes that gap by naming the people who are accountable for each dataset, recording what the datasets are and what they mean, and turning each policy into something the platform enforces and can prove it has enforced.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to assign owner, steward and custodian roles, sort metadata into its three kinds, and turn a policy into a control with a check and evidence.
intro.whyItMatters: A rule that nothing enforces and nobody checks is a hope.

recap.keyIdea: Governance is named owners, stewards and custodians, a catalogue with meaning written in it, and policies turned into enforced and monitored controls.

blocks.text: The owner is accountable for a dataset, the steward maintains its definitions and quality, and the custodian runs the platform. A catalogue holds technical, business and operational metadata, of which only the business kind needs a person to write it.
A policy climbs from rule to control to monitoring to evidence, and a certified dataset is the visible result: owned, defined, tested, fresh, classified and traceable.

questions.prompt: A table has one row per order line. Order 1001 has two lines, of 20.00 and 30.00, and carries a shipping fee of 5.00, which is copied onto both rows. How does the total of the fee column compare with the fee the customer paid?
hints: Count how many rows carry the fee.
`SUM` adds the value on every row.

acceptedIdeas: It is more than 5.00, because each row adds its own copy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is more than 5.00, because each row adds its own copy

questions.onCorrect: The fee was charged once, but the column repeats it on each line, so a sum over lines returns 10.00 instead of 5.00.

misconceptions.feedback: The fee was charged once, but the column holds it on both rows, and a sum adds the value on every row, so the total comes to 10.00.
Nothing divides the fee between the lines. Each row holds the whole 5.00, so a sum over the two rows gives 10.00.

choices.label: It equals the 5.00 that was charged
It is more than 5.00, because each row adds its own copy
It is less than 5.00, because the fee is shared between the lines

questions.prompt: The grain is one row per order line. Which of these columns is not true at that grain?
hints: Ask of each column whether it describes one line or the whole order.

acceptedIdeas: Number of lines on the order
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Number of lines on the order

questions.onCorrect: The number of lines describes the order as a whole, so it repeats on every line and belongs in a table with order grain.

misconceptions.feedback: Each line has its own quantity, so it is true at the line grain.
Each line has its own unit price, so it is true at the line grain.
Each line has its own amount, quantity times unit price, so it is true at the line grain.

choices.label: Unit price
Line amount
Quantity ordered
Number of lines on the order

questions.prompt: Why is each order total added once for every line the order has?
hints: Think about how many rows an order with three lines occupies.

acceptedIdeas: `SUM` adds every row, and each row repeats its order's total
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SUM adds every row, and each row repeats its order's total

questions.onCorrect: An order with three lines contributes three rows, each carrying its total, so the total is counted three times.

misconceptions.feedback: `SUM` does not look at the orders. It adds each row it is given once.
The data type plays no part. The same number simply sits on several rows.
No join is involved here. The repetition is in the table itself.

choices.label: The orders were joined to the wrong table, so some rows were matched twice
`SUM` adds every order twice by default, so each total is doubled
The order total is a different data type, so `SUM` handles it differently
`SUM` adds every row, and each row repeats its order's total

questions.prompt: Orders of 50, 70 and 90 have 2, 4 and 1 lines, and each line row repeats its order total. What does `SUM(order_total)` over the line table return?
hints: Multiply each order total by its number of lines.
Do that for all three orders.
Add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: The line table counts each order once per line, so the sum is 470 although the orders came to 210.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the three orders, 50 + 70 + 90. The line table repeats each total once per line.
That counts the lines. The column holds the order totals, which are added up.

questions.prompt: An inventory fact table has three dimensions: date, warehouse and product. How is each fact row connected to its context?
hints: Ask what a single sale has to be attached to.
In a star, every dimension is joined directly to the fact table.

acceptedIdeas: It holds one foreign key for each dimension, three in all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It holds one foreign key for each dimension, three in all

questions.onCorrect: Each fact row points at exactly one row in each dimension, so it holds three foreign keys, which is what gives the diagram its star shape.

misconceptions.feedback: In a star the dimensions are not linked to each other. Each fact row points directly at one row in every dimension, so it needs a key for each of the three.
Copying the descriptive columns onto every fact row would repeat them millions of times. The fact row keeps one key per dimension and the description stays in the dimension table.
A dimension row describes one customer or one product and is shared by many fact rows, so it cannot hold their keys. The fact row points at the dimension, one key for each.

choices.label: It holds one foreign key to the date dimension, which links on to the others
It holds copies of every column from the three dimensions
It holds no keys, because each dimension row points at its fact rows
It holds one foreign key for each dimension, three in all

questions.prompt: Each order carries a shipping fee of 5.00, copied onto every line row. Order 1 has 4 lines and order 2 has 1 line. By how much does `SUM(fee)` over the line table exceed the fees actually charged?
hints: Work out the sum over lines first.
Then work out what was really charged, once per order.
Subtract the second from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The table sums 5.00 × 4 + 5.00 × 1 = 25.00, while 2 fees were charged: 10.00. The excess is 15.00.

questions.onCorrect: Moving the fee to an order table would sum to 10.00 exactly, since each order then has one row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum over the line table. The question asks how far it is above the fees charged.
That is the fees actually charged, 2 × 5.00, not the excess.

questions.prompt: Which is a well-formed grain statement for a sales fact table?
hints: A grain statement says what one row stands for.
Look for the one that you could use to count the rows.

acceptedIdeas: One row per product on each receipt line
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One row per product on each receipt line

questions.onCorrect: Only the third says what one row is, which tells you what a count of rows would mean.

misconceptions.feedback: A word like this names a topic but does not say what one row is.
This names a period, but a row could be a store, a product or a till.
Everything about customers is a subject, not the definition of a row.

choices.label: Daily sales data
Sales
Everything about customers
One row per product on each receipt line

questions.prompt: Orders of 100, 200 and 300 have 2, 1 and 3 order lines. An `order_total` column is copied onto each line. What does `SUM(order_total)` over the line table return?
hints: Each total appears once for every line.
Multiply each order total by its line count.
Add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: The sum counts each order once per line, so it overstates the 600 of the orders by 700.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the three orders. The line table repeats each total once per line.
That counts the lines. The column being summed holds the totals.

questions.prompt: "How long does it take to ship an order after payment?" Which business process does the model record? Answer in two words.
hints: Which activity packs and ships what was ordered?
The process is named for the activity, not for the table.
questions.onCorrect: Fulfilment leaves a payment time and a shipped time, so it can answer how long shipping takes.

misconceptions.feedback: Order taking records what was bought and at what price. It does not record when the parcel left.

questions.prompt: Stock of product P1 closed at 40 on Monday, 35 on Tuesday and 50 on Wednesday. A report adds the three figures and labels the result as the stock for the three days. How does that total compare with the stock the warehouse actually held?
hints: Ask whether Tuesday's stock is new units or mostly Monday's units still on the shelf.

acceptedIdeas: It is far more than the warehouse ever held at once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is far more than the warehouse ever held at once

questions.onCorrect: The total is 125, although the warehouse never held more than 50, because the same units are counted again on each day they stay on the shelf.

misconceptions.feedback: The three figures add up to 125, while the warehouse never held more than 50, because most of Tuesday's units were already counted on Monday.
Adding three positive figures cannot give less than any one of them. The total is 125, against at most 50 in the warehouse on any day.

choices.label: It is about the same as the stock the warehouse held on any one day
It is less than the stock on Wednesday
It is far more than the warehouse ever held at once

questions.prompt: A daily conversion rate, orders divided by site visits, is stored on each row of a fact table. Which kind of measure is it? Answer with the one word or hyphenated name.
hints: Additive measures sum across every dimension, and semi-additive ones across all but time.
A rate, like a percentage, does not add up across any dimension.
questions.onCorrect: A rate of this kind is a ratio, so it has to be rebuilt from additive parts, here orders and visits.

misconceptions.feedback: Semi-additive measures, like balances, still add across some dimensions. A rate adds across none.
Adding two days' conversion rates gives a number that is not the conversion rate of either day or of both.

questions.prompt: Why is the average of 25% and 50% a poor margin for the two lines together?
hints: Compare the revenue of the two lines.

acceptedIdeas: It gives the small line the same weight as the large one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It gives the small line the same weight as the large one

questions.onCorrect: Each percentage divides by its own revenue, so adding the parts first and dividing once keeps the weights right.

misconceptions.feedback: SQL can average any number. The fault is in the meaning of the result.
Different costs are normal. The point is that each percentage is a ratio of different totals.
The size of a percentage does not stop it being averaged. The weights are the trouble.

choices.label: It gives the small line the same weight as the large one
SQL cannot average percentages, so the figure would be an error
A margin of 50% is too large to be averaged with a smaller one
The two lines have different costs, so their margins cannot be combined

questions.prompt: Two sales lines sold 10 units for 300 in revenue and 5 units for 100 in revenue. What is the overall average unit price, to two decimal places?
hints: Sum the additive parts first.
Total revenue over total quantity.
400 divided by 15.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue is 300 + 100 = 400 and quantity is 10 + 5 = 15, so 400 / 15 = 26.67.

questions.onCorrect: Unit price is rebuilt from two additive measures, which is why the fact table stores revenue and quantity.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the two prices, 30 and 20, and gives the five-unit line the same weight as the ten-unit one.
That is the total revenue. The price is revenue divided by quantity.

questions.prompt: A table holds one row per bank account at the end of each month, giving the balance, including months with no transactions. Which type of fact table is it?
hints: The row exists for every month, whether or not anything happened.
Look at the state, not the event.
questions.onCorrect: A periodic snapshot records state at regular intervals, which suits levels such as stock and balances.

misconceptions.feedback: A transaction fact records events. A month with no transactions would have no row, so the balance could not be read from it.

questions.prompt: The shop system has customers 3, 4 and 8, and the web system has customers 3 and 8. Each system numbers its own customers, so no customer appears in both. How many rows does `dim_customer` hold?
hints: Count people, not ids.
Each system numbers its own customers.
Three shop customers and two web customers are all different people.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five different people give five rows, each with its own surrogate key.

questions.onCorrect: A surrogate key lets the two 3s and the two 8s coexist, since the warehouse numbers rows itself.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the distinct source ids, 3, 4 and 8, but a shared id belongs to two different people.
That counts the web system only. Both systems feed the dimension.

questions.prompt: An accumulating snapshot tracks orders through ordered, paid, shipped and delivered. Three orders have each passed all four milestones. How many rows does the table hold?
hints: Check the grain: what does one row stand for?
One row stands for one order.
Count the orders, not the milestones.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One row per order, updated at each milestone: 3 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The row keeps changing as the order progresses, which is what separates it from a transaction fact.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one row per milestone. The grain is one row per order, which is updated.
That counts the milestones. The rows are orders.

questions.prompt: Which measure is semi-additive?
hints: Which of these is a level at a moment, not an amount of activity?
questions.onCorrect: A balance adds across accounts on one day, but adding it across days gives a figure that means nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: Quantity sold adds across every dimension, time included.
Unit price is a ratio and does not add across any dimension.
Margin percentage is a ratio and does not add across any dimension.

choices.label: Margin percentage
Account balance
Quantity sold
Unit price

questions.prompt: An account's balance was 100 on Monday, 120 on Tuesday and 90 on Wednesday. What is its balance for the period, taking the end-of-period value?
hints: End of period means the last day.
Read off Wednesday.
Do not add or average the three days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The end-of-period value is the last day's balance, 90.

questions.onCorrect: For a balance the end-of-period value is 90, the average would be 103.33, and the sum of 310 means nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three days, which a balance does not allow.
That is the average, not the end-of-period value.

questions.prompt: Which fact table type has one row per order, updated as the order moves through paid, shipped and delivered?
hints: The row is revisited as milestones are reached.
The name says the row accumulates dates.
questions.onCorrect: The row is created when the order is placed and filled in as each milestone arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: A transaction fact is added once and not revisited.
A periodic snapshot adds a row each period instead of updating one.

questions.prompt: Representative R1 sold 40 on 10 January and 60 on 14 February, then moved from North to South on 1 March and sold 25 on 5 April. R2 sold 30 in the North on 6 April. The region column on R1's dimension row is overwritten, so R1 reads South. What happens to R1's January and February sales in a report by region?
hints: The fact rows hold R1's key, not a region.
Ask what the one dimension row for R1 says after the update.

acceptedIdeas: They move to the South along with R1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They move to the South along with R1

questions.onCorrect: Every sale of R1 now joins to a row that says South, so the North shows only R2's 30 and the South shows 125.

misconceptions.feedback: The fact rows hold only R1's key, and the dimension row for that key now says South, so every sale of R1 is reported there and the North shows only R2's 30.
R1 has a single dimension row, and it now says South, so each sale joins to one region only, the South.

choices.label: They move to the South along with R1
They are counted under both regions
They stay in the North, where they were made

questions.prompt: Under a Type 2 design, customer C5 is loaded with the city Leeds, moves to York and later moves again to Hull. How many rows does `dim_customer` hold for C5?
hints: A design that keeps every version holds one row per version.
Count the versions of C5.
Each city C5 has lived in is a version.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One row for each city, Leeds, York and Hull: 3 rows.

questions.onCorrect: Each change adds a row with its own surrogate key and validity dates, so history is kept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Type 1, where the old row is overwritten.
That counts the two moves, but the first version, Leeds, is a row as well.

questions.prompt: Representative R5 moves from West to East. R5's West row runs from 2025-04-01 to 2026-07-01 and the East row from 2026-07-01 to 9999-12-31. A sale is made on exactly 2026-07-01. With `valid_from` included and `valid_to` excluded, which rows does the sale match?
hints: `valid_from` is included and `valid_to` is excluded.
Test the date against each row's two bounds in turn.
questions.onCorrect: One range finishes where the next begins, so a sale on the change date matches exactly one row, the one that starts that day.

misconceptions.feedback: The West row's `valid_to` is 2026-07-01, and the end date is excluded, so the West row stops just before the sale's date.
That happens only when the end date is included. With `valid_to` excluded, the West row stops just before 1 July, so the sale cannot match it.
The East row's `valid_from` is 2026-07-01, and the start date is included, so the East row covers the sale.

choices.label: Only the West row
Only the East row
Neither row
Both rows

questions.prompt: Why does R5's July sale of 50 go to the East row?
hints: Compare the date with each row's range.

acceptedIdeas: 10 July lies in the half-open range that starts on 1 July
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 10 July lies in the half-open range that starts on 1 July

questions.onCorrect: The sale date must be on or after `valid_from` and before `valid_to`, and only one row satisfies both.

misconceptions.feedback: The key plays no part. The date range decides.
East is R5's region today, but the join uses the date of each sale, which is why the June sale of 45 still finds the West row.
The join does not pick the newest row, since the June sale of 45 finds the West row.

choices.label: East is the current region of R5, so the join uses the current row
The East row has the highest key, so the join takes the latest version
July sales always go to the newest row, whichever dates it covers
10 July lies in the half-open range that starts on 1 July

questions.prompt: Representative R3 was in West until 2026-02-01 and in East from that date on, with `valid_to` excluded. R3 sold 10 on 2026-01-05, 20 on 2026-02-01 and 35 on 2026-03-15. R4 is always in East and sold 5 on 2026-03-20. What is East's total in an as-of join?
hints: Decide for each sale which row its date falls in.
2026-02-01 belongs to the East row.
Add the East sales: R3's later two and R4's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sale of 10 is in West. 20, 35 and 5 fall in East: 20 + 35 + 5 = 60.

questions.onCorrect: The sale on the change date belongs to the new version, and the January sale stays with West.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the sale on 2026-02-01, which is on the East row's first day and so belongs to it.
That includes the sale of 10 from January, which was made while R3 was in West.

questions.prompt: A sales fact table and a returns fact table both join the same `dim_product`, with the same keys and meaning. What is such a shared dimension called?
hints: The word describes dimensions that agree across fact tables.
It starts with "conform".
questions.onCorrect: Because both facts use identical product keys, sales and returns can be compared by product.

misconceptions.feedback: A surrogate key identifies a row. The shared dimension as a whole is something else.

questions.prompt: A customer's phone number was keyed wrongly and has been corrected in the source system. Nobody needs the wrong number, so history is not wanted. Which slowly changing dimension type fits?
hints: Ask whether the old value was ever true.
questions.onCorrect: Overwriting suits a correction, since the old value was never true and no past fact should remember it.

misconceptions.feedback: A new row would keep the wrong number as a version that past facts point at, which is history nobody wants for a typing error.
A column for the previous value keeps one step of history, and here the previous value is a mistake with no use to any report.

choices.label: Type 3: add a column for the previous number
Type 1: overwrite the number
Type 2: add a new row with validity dates

questions.prompt: Setup: `CREATE TABLE dim_customer(sk INT, cust_id TEXT, city TEXT, valid_from TEXT, valid_to TEXT);` `INSERT INTO dim_customer VALUES (1,'C1','Leeds','2025-01-01','2026-03-01'),(2,'C1','York','2026-03-01','9999-12-31'),(3,'C2','Leeds','2025-01-01','9999-12-31');` `CREATE TABLE sales(id INT,cust_id TEXT,sale_date TEXT,amount INT);` `INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,'C1','2026-01-15',50),(2,'C1','2026-02-20',30),(3,'C1','2026-04-02',70),(4,'C2','2026-04-03',20);` Join `sales` to `dim_customer` on `cust_id` with `sale_date >= valid_from AND sale_date < valid_to`. What is the York total?
hints: Match each sale to the row whose range holds its date.
C1's first two sales are before 2026-03-01.
Add the sales that land on a York row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the sale of 70 on 2026-04-02 falls in the York row, which starts on 2026-03-01: 70.

questions.onCorrect: The as-of join sends each sale to the version valid on its date, so only the April sale counts as York.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the York total for a join to current rows only. Here each sale uses the row valid on its date.
That is the Leeds total.

questions.prompt: With the same tables, join only to the current rows (`valid_to = '9999-12-31'`). What is the York total?
hints: Which row is current for C1?
Every C1 sale joins to that one row.
Add C1's three sales.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: C1's current row is York, so all three of C1's sales, 50 + 30 + 70, land on it: 150.

questions.onCorrect: Joining to current rows only puts every past sale under the present attribute, which is the error Type 2 prevents.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the as-of total. Here every C1 sale joins to the current York row.
That is the Leeds total under a current-row join.

questions.prompt: Finance must report each past sale under the sales region the account manager belonged to at the time, and managers move between regions several times. Which approach fits?
hints: The past must stay readable, and there is more than one move to keep.

acceptedIdeas: Type 2: keep a row for each version, with dates
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Type 2: keep a row for each version, with dates

questions.onCorrect: Type 2 keeps every version with its dates, so each sale joins to the region valid on its date.

misconceptions.feedback: Type 0 never changes an attribute after loading, so every sale would stay under the first region and miss each later move.
Overwriting loses the region each sale was made under.
A column for the previous region keeps only one step of history, so a manager who moves several times loses the earlier regions.

choices.label: Type 0: never change the region once it is loaded
Type 1: overwrite the region when a manager moves
Type 2: keep a row for each version, with dates
Type 3: add a column for the previous region

questions.prompt: Invoice 1 has total 90 and 3 lines, invoice 2 has total 150 and 2 lines, and invoice 3 has total 40 and 1 line, so the invoices come to 280. Each invoice is joined to its lines and the invoice total is summed over the joined rows. How does `SUM(total)` compare with 280?
hints: Ask how many rows the join returns for invoice 1.
`SUM` adds the total on every joined row.
questions.onCorrect: Each total is added once per line, 90 × 3 + 150 × 2 + 40 × 1, which is 610 against the 280 the invoices came to.

misconceptions.feedback: Every invoice has at least one line, so each one appears in the join. It appears once per line, which makes the sum 610.
The join returns one row per line and copies the invoice total onto each, so invoice 1's total is added three times and the sum comes to 610.

choices.label: It equals 280
It is less than 280, because some invoices drop out of the join
It is more than 280

questions.prompt: Four invoices have 2, 4, 1 and 3 lines. How many rows does the join of invoices to invoice lines return?
hints: A join on a one-to-many key gives one row per child.
Add the line counts.
Compare the result with the 4 invoices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The join returns one row per line, so 2 + 4 + 1 + 3 = 10 rows, while `invoices` has 4.

questions.onCorrect: When the row count after a join is larger than the parent table, the parent rows have been repeated.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of invoices. The join returns one row for each matching line.
That multiplies the counts. A join of this kind returns one row per child row.

questions.prompt: Why does aggregating the lines to one row per invoice before the join keep the total right?
hints: Think about how many rows each invoice matches after the lines are aggregated.

acceptedIdeas: Each invoice then matches exactly one row, so it is not repeated
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each invoice then matches exactly one row, so it is not repeated

questions.onCorrect: A join that matches each parent to one child row cannot repeat the parent.

misconceptions.feedback: The join still runs, but on a child table that has one row per invoice.
`SUM` adds every row it is given, repeated or not.
The invoice total is read from `invoices` as before; nothing is recalculated.

choices.label: `SUM` ignores repeated rows, so the repeats do no harm
Each invoice then matches exactly one row, so it is not repeated
The invoice total is recalculated from the lines, so it always matches
The join is skipped, so no rows can be repeated

questions.prompt: Orders 1, 2 and 3 have totals of 80, 120 and 50 and are joined to payments that have been aggregated to one row per order. What does `SUM(total)` over the joined result return?
hints: After aggregation each order matches one row.
Nothing is repeated.
Add the three totals.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With one payment row per order each order is matched once, so the sum is 80 + 120 + 50 = 250.

questions.onCorrect: Aggregating the many side to the parent's grain first is the standard repair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum when payments are not aggregated: 80 × 2 + 120 × 1 + 50 × 4.
That counts the orders. The column holds their totals.

questions.prompt: A marketing team's email tool reads a single table with one row per customer, and each row already carries the customer's region, last order date and total spend, so the tool never joins anything. Which shape is that? Answer with its usual name.
hints: It trades repeated data for having no joins.
The shape puts everything on every row.
questions.onCorrect: A wide table suits one purpose well, but it repeats data and hides the grain, so it is built last from a star.

misconceptions.feedback: A star keeps the dimensions in separate tables, so it needs joins.

questions.prompt: A data vault holds two hubs, customer and product, one link between them for order lines, and one satellite for each hub. How many tables is that in all?
hints: Count hubs, links and satellites separately.
Two hubs and one link make three.
Add the two satellites.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 hubs + 1 link + 2 satellites = 5 tables.

questions.onCorrect: A vault has more tables than the star built from it, which is the price of its auditability.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts hubs and the link but leaves out the satellites.
That leaves out one of the satellites, or counts one hub too few.

questions.prompt: A data vault has a hub for students and a hub for courses. Each enrolment records that a student took a course. Which kind of table holds that relationship?
hints: A vault has three kinds of table: hubs, links and satellites.

acceptedIdeas: A link between the two hubs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A link between the two hubs

questions.onCorrect: A link records a relationship between hubs, and satellites on the link can then hold the enrolment's own attributes, such as its grade.

misconceptions.feedback: A satellite holds descriptive attributes of one hub, with their load dates. A relationship between two hubs is held in a link.
A hub holds only the business keys of one kind of thing. A relationship between a student and a course is held in a link that points at both hubs.
A wide table is a reporting shape, not part of a vault. Inside the vault a relationship between hubs is held in a link.

choices.label: A third hub for enrolments
A wide table of students and courses
A satellite on the student hub
A link between the two hubs

questions.prompt: Customer 1 has a credit limit of 500 and 3 orders, and customer 2 has a limit of 800 and 2 orders. The customers are joined to their orders and the credit limit is summed. What does `SUM(credit_limit)` return?
hints: The measure belongs to the customer, not the order.
Multiply each limit by its order count.
Add the two products.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 × 3 + 800 × 2 = 1,500 + 1,600 = 3,100, against 1,300 for the customers alone.

questions.onCorrect: Any customer attribute, not only money, is repeated once per order after the join.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum on customers alone. After the join each limit repeats once per order.
That counts the orders. The column holds credit limits.

questions.prompt: Setup: `CREATE TABLE o(id INT, total INT);` `INSERT INTO o VALUES (1,100),(2,200),(3,300);` `CREATE TABLE i(oid INT, sku TEXT);` `INSERT INTO i VALUES (1,'a'),(1,'b'),(2,'c'),(3,'a'),(3,'b'),(3,'c');` What does `SELECT SUM(o.total) FROM o JOIN i ON i.oid = o.id` return?
hints: Count the items of each order in i.
Each total repeats once per item.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 1, 2 and 3 have 2, 1 and 3 items, so the sum is 100 × 2 + 200 × 1 + 300 × 3 = 1,300.

questions.onCorrect: The join has six rows, one per item, and each carries its order's total.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum on o alone. After the join each order repeats once per item.
That is the number of joined rows.

questions.prompt: With the same tables, what does `SELECT SUM(total) FROM o` return?
hints: No join this time.
Each order appears once.
Add the three totals.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sum is over `o` alone, with one row per order: 100 + 200 + 300 = 600.

questions.onCorrect: Summing at the grain of o, before any join to i, avoids the repetition.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum after joining to i, where totals repeat.
That counts items, not totals.

questions.prompt: Which shape fits integrating ten source systems with full audit history before building reports?
hints: Integration and reporting need different shapes.

acceptedIdeas: A data vault feeding dimensional marts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A data vault feeding dimensional marts

questions.onCorrect: The vault integrates and keeps history, and the dimensional marts built on it serve reporting.

misconceptions.feedback: A wide table hides the source of each value and cannot keep audit history.
Marts built straight from each source repeat the integration in every mart, and nothing keeps what each source said at the time.
Normalised tables alone leave every report to chain joins and give no layer for audit.

choices.label: One big table that combines every source system
Dimensional marts built straight from each source
A data vault feeding dimensional marts
Normalised tables only, with reports chaining the joins

questions.prompt: Seven models each read the table `raw.orders` directly by its name, and each renames its columns in its own way. The source table is then renamed `raw.orders_v2`. Which models have to be edited?
hints: Ask where the table's name is written down.
questions.onCorrect: Each model names the table itself, so each has to change, and nothing makes the seven edits agree with one another.

misconceptions.feedback: A model that names a table in its SQL looks for that exact name when it runs, so after the rename every one of them fails until it is edited.
Each of the seven names `raw.orders` itself, so the order in which they were written makes no difference, and every one of them has to change.

choices.label: All seven
Only the first model that was written
None, since the warehouse follows the new name

questions.prompt: A model joins `stg_shipments` to `stg_orders` to give one row per shipment with its order date. Which layer is it in? Answer with the layer name.
hints: It reshapes data from staging models and is not the finished table.
It is neither the first step nor the last.
questions.onCorrect: Intermediate models join and reshape, and the marts that read them are the finished tables.

misconceptions.feedback: A staging model reads one source and changes nothing but names and types. Joining belongs one layer later.
A mart is the finished table for use. This join is a step on the way to one.

questions.prompt: A model has 2,000,000,000 rows and gains 5,000,000 new ones each hour. How many times more rows does a full rebuild process in an hour than an incremental run that handles only the new rows?
hints: Divide the size of the table by the size of an hourly batch.
Cancel six zeros from each.
questions.onCorrect: The saving grows with the table: the full rebuild repeats work on rows that cannot have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio the other way round, the incremental run over the full rebuild.
Check the zeros: 2,000,000,000 has nine and 5,000,000 has six, so the quotient has three digits.

questions.prompt: In the graph, how many models, counting only models and not the raw sources, must be built before `fct_orders` can run?
hints: Start from `fct_orders` and go back along the arrows.
Its two direct parents are intermediate models.
Add the staging models they read.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `fct_orders` reads `int_orders_joined` and `int_payments_by_order`, which read `stg_customers`, `stg_orders` and `stg_payments`: 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: The tool follows the arrows back from a model to work out everything that must run first.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only its direct parents. Their own parents must run first too.
That counts every model. `dim_customers` and `rpt_daily_revenue` are not needed.

questions.prompt: Why can `stg_orders` and `stg_payments` be built in the same round?
hints: What would stop one running before the other?
questions.onCorrect: Models that have no path between them can run in any order, so the tool can run them together.

misconceptions.feedback: Being a view does not decide order. A view can depend on another model.
The layer does not decide it. Dependence does.
The columns play no part. The arrows decide.

choices.label: Both are in the staging layer
They have the same number of columns
Both are views
Neither depends on the other

questions.prompt: A new model, `int_refunds`, reads `stg_payments` and feeds `fct_orders`. Besides it, `fct_orders` still reads what it did before. How many models must now run before `fct_orders`?
hints: Start from the five that ran before.
`int_refunds` is one new model.
`stg_payments` was already counted.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The earlier five plus `int_refunds` make 6.

questions.onCorrect: A new model adds only the models that are not already upstream, and `stg_payments` was.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before `int_refunds` was added.
`int_refunds` reads `stg_payments`, which is already counted, so only one model is added.

questions.prompt: In the model graph, if `stg_customers` changes, how many models downstream of it, directly or indirectly, have to be rebuilt?
hints: Follow the arrows forward from `stg_customers`.
Two models read it directly.
Add the models that read those.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `int_orders_joined` and `dim_customers` read it, `fct_orders` reads the first, and `rpt_daily_revenue` reads that: 4.

questions.onCorrect: The same graph answers both questions, what must run first and what is affected, which is the idea behind lineage.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only its direct children. Their children are affected too.
That leaves out `rpt_daily_revenue`, which reads `fct_orders`.

questions.prompt: Where should casting amount from text to a decimal and renaming `orderid` to `order_id` happen? Name the layer.
hints: Which layer mirrors one source and changes only names and types?
Doing it once, early, means every model after it sees the same clean columns.
questions.onCorrect: Staging models mirror one source each, so every later model sees the same cleaned columns.

misconceptions.feedback: A mart is the finished table. Casting there means every other model has to repeat it.

questions.prompt: A model with several billion rows grows by appending new events each hour. Which materialisation suits it? Answer in one or two words.
hints: The table is large and only gains new rows.
Rebuilding every row each hour repeats work on rows that cannot change.
questions.onCorrect: An incremental table adds only the new rows each run, so the cost follows the new data and not the whole table.

misconceptions.feedback: A view would re-run the whole query on every read, over billions of rows.
A plain table would be rebuilt in full every hour.
An ephemeral model is never stored, so billions of rows would be recomputed in each model that used it.

questions.prompt: In dbt, which function does one model use to refer to another so that the tool can order the build? Give the function name.
hints: It takes the name of the model as its argument.
It is a function that takes a model name and gives back the table to read.
questions.onCorrect: The tool reads every ref call to build the graph, so the order and the lineage come from the code itself.

misconceptions.feedback: The source function points at raw tables outside the project, not at other models.

questions.prompt: A target holds three invoices, and the latest `updated_at` in it is 2026-06-10. The source holds six: id 1 on 06-08, id 2 on 06-11, id 3 on 06-10, id 4 on 06-09, id 5 on 06-11 and id 6 on 06-12. A run reads only rows with `updated_at` later than the latest in the target. How many of the six source rows does it read?
hints: Compare each row's date with 06-10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ids 2, 5 and 6 are stamped after 06-10, so the run reads 3 of the 6 rows.

questions.onCorrect: Three rows, ids 2, 5 and 6, are stamped after 06-10, so the run reads three of the six and skips the rest.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the whole source. The filter keeps only rows stamped after 06-10, and ids 1, 3 and 4 are stamped on or before that date, so they are skipped.
That counts id 3 as well, but id 3 is stamped 06-10, which is the cut-off itself and not later than it.
Ids 2, 5 and 6 are stamped 06-11 and 06-12, after the target's latest timestamp, so the filter reads them.

questions.prompt: Before the run the target holds three rows. The run reads ids 2, 5 and 6 and merges them into the target by id. Id 2 already exists there, and ids 5 and 6 do not. How many rows does the target hold afterwards?
hints: An existing id is updated, not added again.
Two ids are new.
Add them to the three that were there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 2 is updated in place and ids 5 and 6 are added, so 3 + 2 = 5 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The merge is by key, so a changed row replaces its old version and new ones are added.

misconceptions.feedback: Id 4 was not read, so it is not in the target.
That is the target before the run. Two new ids are added.

questions.prompt: The target holds ids 1 to 4, and its latest `updated_at` is 2026-07-20. The source also has id 3 changed on 07-21, id 5 stamped 07-18 but added after the target was loaded, and id 6 stamped 07-22. Each run reads only rows later than the target's latest timestamp. Which row is never loaded?
hints: Look for a row stamped before the cut-off that is not yet in the target.
questions.onCorrect: Id 5 carries a date older than the target's latest, and the latest can only grow, so no later run will read it either.

misconceptions.feedback: Id 3 is stamped 07-21, after the cut-off, so the run reads it and the merge replaces the old version in the target.
Id 6 is stamped 07-22, after the cut-off, so the run reads it and adds it to the target.

choices.label: Id 6
Id 5
Id 3

questions.prompt: Why does re-reading id 3 with a lookback not create a duplicate row?
hints: What does the merge compare to decide a row already exists?

acceptedIdeas: The merge matches on the unique key and updates the row
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The merge matches on the unique key and updates the row

questions.onCorrect: A unique key lets a re-read row replace itself, which is what makes a lookback safe.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing removes rows first. The merge replaces the matching row.
Id 3 is read, and the merge matches it by key. The data being unchanged is not why.
The filter does not look at the target's rows, only its latest timestamp.

choices.label: The target deletes the old rows before the new ones are written
The filter drops rows that are already loaded before the merge
The merge matches on the unique key and updates the row
Id 3 is ignored because its values have not changed

questions.prompt: The source rows are id 1 at 09-15, id 2 at 09-21, id 3 at 09-18, id 4 at 09-20, id 5 at 09-18 and id 6 at 09-22. With a lookback of 2 days the filter reads rows with `updated_at` later than 2026-09-18. How many of the six rows does it read?
hints: Compare each date with 2026-09-18.
Strictly later excludes 09-18.
Two rows are stamped exactly 09-18.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ids 2, 4 and 6 are later than 09-18. Ids 3 and 5 are stamped 09-18 exactly and are left out: 3 rows.

questions.onCorrect: A lookback of 2 days still misses the late row, because its timestamp falls on the cut-off, and the window must be longer than the lateness.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts both rows stamped 09-18, but neither is later than the cut-off.
That counts one of the two rows stamped 09-18, but neither is later than the cut-off.

questions.prompt: A model definition is changed so that country is stored as a two-letter code instead of the full name. The target has 8 rows, and the next incremental run reads and rewrites 3 of them. What does the target hold afterwards?
hints: Ask what an incremental run does to the rows it does not read.

acceptedIdeas: Three rows with codes and five with full names
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three rows with codes and five with full names

questions.onCorrect: The new logic reaches only the rows a run reads, so the table is a mixture until a full refresh rebuilds it.

misconceptions.feedback: An incremental run applies the new logic only to the rows it reads. The other five are left as they were, with full names.
An incremental run keeps the rows it does not read, so all eight remain, five of them still with full names.

choices.label: Three rows, because the run keeps only the rows it rewrote
Three rows with codes and five with full names
All eight rows now hold codes, because the whole table is rebuilt

questions.prompt: A row stamped 2026-06-09 reaches the source after the target's latest `updated_at` has already reached 2026-06-12. The filter reads rows with `updated_at` later than the latest minus N days. What is the smallest whole number N that reads the row?
hints: The row must be strictly later than the cut-off.
Work out the cut-off for N = 3.
Try the next whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 06-12 minus N days must be earlier than 06-09. N = 3 gives 06-09, which is not earlier, so N = 4.

questions.onCorrect: A strict comparison needs a window one day longer than the lateness, which is why a lookback is chosen with some margin.

misconceptions.feedback: N = 3 gives a cut-off of 06-09, and the row is stamped 06-09, which is not later.
That gives a cut-off of 06-10, which is later than the row.

questions.prompt: Setup: `CREATE TABLE tgt(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT, updated_at TEXT);` `INSERT INTO tgt VALUES (1,10,'2026-05-01'),(2,20,'2026-05-02'),(3,30,'2026-05-03');` `CREATE TABLE src(id INT, v INT, updated_at TEXT);` `INSERT INTO src VALUES (1,10,'2026-05-01'),(2,25,'2026-05-04'),(3,30,'2026-05-03'),(4,40,'2026-05-04'),(5,50,'2026-05-02');` Merge rows with `updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM tgt)` into `tgt` by `id`. How many rows does `tgt` hold afterwards?
hints: Find the latest `updated_at` in `tgt`.
Read the source rows later than that.
One id updates an existing row and one adds a new row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The filter reads ids 2 and 4. Id 2 replaces its old row and id 4 is added, so tgt holds ids 1, 2, 3 and 4: 4 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The filter reads ids 2 and 4, and the merge updates one row and adds one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts id 5, which is stamped 05-02, earlier than the latest in tgt, so it is not read.
That is tgt before the run. One more row is added.

questions.prompt: Which source id is never loaded by that filter? Give the id.
hints: Look for a source row that is not in tgt.
Its timestamp must be older than the target's latest.
Only one such row exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 5 is stamped 2026-05-02, which is earlier than the target's latest, 2026-05-03, so the filter never reads it.

questions.onCorrect: A row with an old timestamp that appears after the target has moved on is skipped for good.

misconceptions.feedback: That row is later than the target's latest, so it is read.
Id 1 is already in the target.

questions.prompt: Which technique, re-reading a recent window of rows and merging them on the unique key, picks up late-arriving rows? Answer in one or two words.
hints: The window reaches back from the latest timestamp.
It is named for looking back over recent rows.
questions.onCorrect: A lookback re-reads recent rows, and the unique key keeps the re-read from duplicating them.

misconceptions.feedback: A full refresh rebuilds everything, which also catches late rows but costs the whole build.

questions.prompt: Seven employees have these emails: ana, bo, missing, bo, eli, fay and missing. A unique test returns one row for each email value that appears more than once, ignoring missing values. What does it return?
hints: Leave the missing values aside and look for an email that appears twice.
questions.onCorrect: The missing emails are a separate fault, which a `not_null` test reports, so each test names one assumption.

misconceptions.feedback: Bo appears twice, and that is exactly what a unique test looks for, so it returns a row.
The test ignores missing values, so the two missing emails are not treated as a repeat. Finding them is the job of a `not_null` test.
The test groups the emails and returns one row for each repeated value, not one for each employee who has it.

choices.label: Nothing, so the test passes
One row, for bo
Two rows, one for bo and one for the missing emails
Four rows, one for each employee whose email is repeated

questions.prompt: Eight suppliers have the contact emails kim, missing, lee, missing, max, missing, ola and lee. How many rows does a `not_null` test on `email` return?
hints: The test returns rows where the value is missing.
Look for missing emails.
Count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The test returns the rows whose email is missing, the second, fourth and sixth suppliers, so 3 rows.

questions.onCorrect: A `not_null` test returns the offending rows themselves, so you can see which suppliers lack an email.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the repeated email. A `not_null` test looks for missing values.
That adds the repeated email. The test returns only the rows with a missing email.

questions.prompt: The `departments` table holds ids 10, 20 and 30. Seven employees have the dept_ids 10, 40, missing, 30, 50, missing and 20. How many rows does a `relationships` test on `dept_id` return?
hints: Which dept_ids are not in `departments`?
A missing value does not point at anything.
Count the ones that point at a missing department.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dept_ids 40 and 50 point at departments that do not exist. The two missing dept_ids are not broken references: 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: A relationships test returns rows that point at a parent that is not there, and it skips missing keys.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the missing dept_ids as broken references. A missing value points at nothing, so a `not_null` test is the one to catch it.
Dept_ids 40 and 50 are not in departments.

questions.prompt: Why does the `relationships` test leave out rows whose `invoice_id` is missing?
hints: Is a reference that was never made a broken reference?

acceptedIdeas: A missing value points at no parent, so no reference is broken
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A missing value points at no parent, so no reference is broken

questions.onCorrect: Whether a key may be missing is a separate rule, which a `not_null` test states.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing value equals nothing, not everything.
The join can read it, but a missing key matches no row, which is why the filter is added.
The `unique` test skips missing values too. A missing key is reported by a `not_null` test.

choices.label: The join cannot read `NULL`, so those rows would make the query fail
A missing value points at no parent, so no reference is broken
Rows with a missing key are already reported by the `unique` test
`NULL` equals every invoice id, so those rows always find a parent

questions.prompt: Orders have the statuses paid, refunded, shipped, void, paid, refunded and paid. An `accepted_values` test allows paid and shipped only. How many rows does it return?
hints: Mark each status that is not on the list.
Refunded is not allowed here.
Count the orders with a status that is not allowed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two rows are refunded and one is void, none of them on the list, so the test returns 3 rows.

questions.onCorrect: The allowed list is part of the test, so shortening it makes more rows fail.

questions.prompt: North has revenue 700 and 4 distinct customers. South has revenue 300 and 3 distinct customers. Two customers are in both regions. What is the overall revenue per distinct customer?
